content.title: Response to Reviewer Tbtq
content.comment:
Thank you for your thoughtful comments. In the following, we explain how we have updated our paper by addressing the comments.

**Q1: Benchmark is weak. The authors compared the classification accuracy of ROE with COE and QA which have not been reported in any previous publications. This may undermine the efficacy of ROE. Therefore, the authors should consider systematic and fair comparison of the proposed method with previous methods.**

We respectfully disagree that the benchmark is weak. Actually, we implement the three methods (QA, COE, and ROE) onto the same platform (a state-of-the-art conversion method and several event driven datasets), so that they can compare in a fair way. Specifically, the SNN-QA, introduced at the beginning of the experiment section, replicates an algorithm in [1]. COE removes the floor operation in SNN-QA and does not need to pre-configure the quantization length in training, which eliminates the impact of quantisation on event-based input.

In terms of the comparison results, we also show that ROE can achieve better performance than [2] in Table 2, which applied conversion method on event-based dataset without ROE, QA and COE.

**Q2: Regarding the confidence rate evaluation, I assume that $g(x)$ should be known a priori for all samples to evaluate the confidence rate. That is, this method cannot be used for any test datasets whose $g(x)$ are not available a priori, which significantly undermines the value of the proposed early termination method. Therefore, the proposed early termination method has a certain limitation.**

Theoretically, $g(X)$ is based on the data distribution so we do not know in prior. However, like  most of the machine learning problems, in practice (and in our experiments), we estimate it with a set of data instances sampled from the data distribution.

**Q3: Conversion method is not elaborated. The authors should detail the objective function minimization sequence and all related sub-methods. Particularly, ROE minimization method should be detailed.**

As stated in the paper, for the limitation of spaces we inherit the conversion method and most of the notations from [3] and [1]. Particularly, the relationship between ReLU and IF is from [3] and the relationship between quantised ReLU and IF is from [1]. Moreover, ROE minimisation is based on [3] and operates as a penalty term during ANN training. In the revised manuscript, we have included in the Appendix all the necessary materials. Thank you for pointing this out. 

[1] Bu, Tong et al. Optimal ANNSNN conversion for high-accuracy and ultra-low-latency spiking neural networks. ICLR 2022. 

[2] Kugele, Alexander et al Efficient processing of spatio-temporal data streams with spiking neural networks. Frontiers in Neuroscience, 2020.

[3] Wu, Dengyu  et al. A little energy goes a long way: Build an energyefficient, accurate spiking neural network from convolutional neural network. Frontiers in neuroscience, 2022.

content.title: Response to Reviewer zEep
content.comment:
**Q1: Overall, the paper applies a lot of prior knowledge and research to the problem of training spiking networks, and goes into explicit detail and proofs for the proposed work. The results show clear improvements over the prior works, although on relatively simple datasets and a simple task (image classification). Also, the proposed method only improves upon prior works when the early cutoff is applied (results without it are mixed). This seems a little surprising that terminating early could have such improvements.**

We appreciate your positive comments, and agree with you that early termination has potential to be applied more widely in the SNN. In the following, we would like to take this opportunity to elicit several settings of our work: 



- Research contributions beyond prior works. Firstly, we design a regulariser to train a low-latency SNN, and support the design with a theoretical analysis. Our Theorem 4.1 suggests that low-latency SNN needs a good distribution of accumulated current, which provides  a new metric to measure the performance of SNN. This is in contrast with previous conversion-based methods [1-3], where the algorithms tend to minimise the Mean Square Error (MSE) between ANN and resulted SNN. Secondly, as a first attempt, the proposed cutoff is hardware-friendly and compatible with different SNN neuron models (e.g. IF and LIF), as long as the prediction is based on the number of output spikes. It also highlights the advantage in SNN, which is more adaptable in inference than traditional ANN. 
    
- Datasets and classification task. Unlike static image dataset, e.g., Cifar10/100, the event-based dataset exhibits two significant features, sparsity and asynchronicity. Together with neuromorphic chip, [4] has shown that these two feastures makes the recognition system consume lower power and have lower latency.  In our work, these unique features are fully utilised by our techniques, i.e.,  regulariser and cutoff. The experimental results show that our approach can improve the performance of SNN for event-based input, in terms of accuracy and latency, which is potential for practical implementation. 

[1] Bu, Tong et al. Optimal ANN-SNN conversion for high-accuracy and ultra-low-latency spiking neural networks. ICLR, 2022.

[2] Deng, Shikuang et al. Optimal conversion of conventional artificial neural networks to spiking neural networks. ICLR, 2021. 

[3] Li, Yuhang et al. A free lunch from ann: Towards efficient, accurate spiking neural networks calibration. ICML, 2021.

[4] Amir, Arnon et al. A low power, fully event-based gesture recognition system. CVPR, 2017.

**Q2: Many symbols are also introduced, and perhaps it would be useful to have a glossary to keep track of them all.**

Thanks. A notation table has been added to the Appendix.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 5NBM (1/2)
content.comment:
We appreciate the insightful comments from you and would like to address your concerns as follows.

**Q1: The neurons do not leak, thus old inputs cannot be forgotten. Maybe this is not an issue with the datasets they used, because the different patterns to be recognized are in different files, and all the potentials are reset in between (right?). However, it could be an issue if deployed in a "streaming" setting where potentials are never reset. Can the authors elaborate on this? In addition, could their approach work with LIF instead of IF?**

Actually, our method can work with "streaming" input, and in the meantime reset the potentials between frames.  We believe the key technical argument can be on whether or not the reset can be implemented in hardware, i.e., whether or not our method is hardware friendly. For this, we would like to refer to a few recent work on implementing SNN in hardware, including [1] and [2]. 

Both work has a flag signal that indicates the beginning or end of input spike train and can be used to achieve 'Reset in between'. %'Reset in between' can be achieved by using the flat signal. The flag signal in [1] can be found in their open-source design, named 'TIME\_TICK'. Moreover, [2] mentioned the flag signal in page 6 with description, suggesting that 

'This signal can be used to reset membrane potentials to zero if required'

Regarding LIF vs IF, our approach consists of ROE and Cutoff. ROE may limit to IF because it is based on ANN-to-SNN conversion, but cutoff can be easily extended to LIF and direct training, as it only cares about the number of output spikes. Actually, ANN-to-SNN conversion is a popular research direction with many papers published in the past years. More importantly, as we have argued in Related Work, leveraging ANN-to-SNN conversion can result in fast response SNN and improve the latency, both of which are required in practical applications such as edge computing

[1] Frenkel, Charlotte et al. ReckOn: A 28nm Sub-mm2 Task-Agnostic Spiking Recurrent Neural Network Processor Enabling On-Chip Learning over Second-Long Timescales. ISSCC, 2022.

[2] Khodamoradi, Alireza  et al. S2n2: A fpga accelerator for streaming spiking neural networks. ACM/SIGDA,  2021.

**Q2: Conversely, IF is the way to go with static images. Could their method work with static images?**

Our method can work with static images, which is not surprising. However, the paper is  focused on the dedicated features of DVS camera inputs (i.e., asynchronicity and sparsity), which we believe contribute as an important -- and specialised -- application scenario for SNNs. 

**Q3: The ANN that is trained ignores the time, in the sense that shuffling the frames in Eq 4 would have no effect on the loss. This wouldn't work on a truly temporal task in which the order of the sequence matter. The most temporal dataset here is DVS Gesture, but even with this one, most gestures can be categorized based on spatial information only (even the clockwise and counterclockwise hand gesture can usually be distinguished if using the event polarities).**

While considering a fully temporal application is tempting, neither ANN nor SNN is designed for it when there is no recurrent mechanism (where there are memory units to store state information) as we do in this paper. By working with non-recurrent SNN, this paper is dealing with the other two important features of DVS, asynchronicity and sparsity, which lead to the lower latency and lower power in recognition system [3], even if the machine learning tasks based on DVS input are not necessarily fully temporal. As the evidence to demonstrate that these two properties are practically useful, we note that [4] has shown that the object detection with sparse events can be more computational efficiency than the traditional ANN --- dense and synchronous operations. Moreover, these features also encourage the authors in [5] to develop an event-based dataset based on ImageNet.

[3] Amiret, Arnon  et al. A low power, fully event-based gesture recognition system. CVPR,  2017.

[4] Messikommer, Nico et al. Event-based asynchronous sparse convolutional networks. ECCV, 2020.

[5] Kim, Junho et al,  N-imagenet: Towards robust, fine-grained object recognition with event cameras. CVPR, 2021.

content.title: Accuracy is excellent, but the paper is somewhat confusing
content.comment:
Thank you for your answers.
I wasn't aware that you reset all the potentials at each time step!
I see that you now say it in the new version of the manuscript.
Resetting at every timestep is not necessarily a bad idea, but it has a lot of implications that are not discussed:

* Their SNN does not do any temporal integration, therefore it cannot learn temporal dependencies.

* Their SNN can be seen as a feedforward, stateless, ANN that uses Heaviside activation functions (aka McCulloch & Pitts neurons aka threshold gates).

* It can also be seen as semi-quantized ANN, where activations are quantized on one bit, and weights are not quantized.

* Eq 1 is confusing, because V(t-1) is always 0.

* The soft reset that follows firing is unuseful, because the potential will be zeroed for the next time step in any case.

But as I've already said the accuracy they reach is very good!

For all these reasons, my rating is now 6.

content.title: New response to Reviewer 5NBM
content.comment:
We appreciate your increase of rating and the additional comments. We would like to have one more round of discussions with you, as follows. 

**Resetting at every timestep is not necessarily a bad idea, but it has a lot of implications that are not discussed**

Firstly, we need to clarify that $t$ is an analog value, representing time point, which is different from the discrete timestep in prior work. In addition, we use $t$ to multiply with spiking resolution $S_r$ to approximate the timestep that has been introduced in the text below Equation 6. Secondly, frame number $F$ and timestep $tS_r$ are different from each other. Specifically, SNN can have more than one timestep within one frame. We let the duration of one frame be $T$ and the membrane potential could accumulate and reset by subtract though $T$ within each frame. The membrane potential of the hidden layer is reset after each frame, while that of the output layer is reset after the last frame.

We have now updated the statement on "reset to zero" more precise in manuscript.

**Q1: Their SNN does not do any temporal integration, therefore it cannot learn temporal dependencies**

While it is unlikely for SNN/ANN without memory units to deal with temporal dependencies very well, there are two kinds of temporal integration in our SNN as follows 

- Neurons at hidden layer integrate and fire within one frame.

- Neurons at output layer integrate and fire before the last frame. 

**Q2: Their SNN can be seen as a feedforward, stateless, ANN that uses Heaviside activation functions (aka McCulloch \& Pitts neurons aka threshold gates).**

When $F>1$, the membrane potential in output layer can remember the state from previous frames. 

**Q3: It can also be seen as semi-quantized ANN, where activations are quantized on one bit, and weights are not quantized.**

We believe there are major differences with semi-quantized ANN, because in SNN the membrane potential integrates and fires over time.

**Q4-5: Eq 1 is confusing, because V(t-1) is always 0. The soft reset that follows firing is unuseful, because the potential will be zeroed for the next time step in any case.**

V(t-1) and soft reset are needed, as the integrate-and-fire process happens within one frame.

For example, is the activity more sparse? Another contribution would be to understand why spikes are beneficial in this network. **Q1: it would be interesting to understand why the introduction of such mechanisms improves performance, for example by analyzing the statistics of the learned networks, such as the distribution of spike frequencies**

Comparing with QA, ROE helps ANN retain a Gaussian-like distribution. On the other hand, ROE brings the $99.99th$ percentile value closer to the mean of the activation than COE.

For example, from Eq. 4, it is clearly that the ordering of frames does not have an impact on the performance. In addition, Eq. 6 shows that it is the average spiking rate that plays the most important role in classification,  that is, the  ordering between spikes in a frame does  not have a significant impact on the performance.

Weaknesses:
-1. The proposed approach only limits to the IF model, the simplest SNN neuron model. In addition, I disagree that SNNs are just a variant of ANNs. If so, why not just ANNs directly? Why suffer so much, especially for classification tasks?

-2. Leveraging DVS for classification itself does not make much sense. DVS is sensitive to motion, and it can provide rich temporal information but lacks texture cues. The classification does not require temporal information but requires texture cues. 

-3. The author claimed that they directly process the raw events in an asynchronous manner. But, it is not clear to me how did authors achieve it. 

-4. In section 4.1, the authors claimed, "When t is large enough to make ∆l(t) negligible," but why? 

-5. For ROE, $A^l$ represents a batch of $a^l$ during training. Then, it means the batch size could impact the performance of the trained model. However, the authors did not show any experimental results about it.

-6. The author should provide experimental results to prove Theorem 4.1. I expect the experimental results also show the positive correlation between classification accuracy and $(\sqrt{n_l}\frac{V_{the}^l}{||a^l||_2})^{-1}$.

content.title: Response to Reviewer ozZz (1/2)
content.comment:
Thank you for your thoughtful comments. We would like to address your concerns and your questions in the following.

__Q1: The proposed approach only limits to the IF model, the simplest SNN neuron model. In addition, I disagree that SNNs are just a variant of ANNs. If so, why not just ANNs directly? Why suffer so much, especially for classification tasks?__

This paper includes two main techniques: ROE and Cutoff. It is true that ROE is for IF because it is based on ANN-to-SNN conversion, but cutoff can be easily extended to LIF and direct training, as it simply deals with the number of output spikes. Actually, ANN-to-SNN conversion is a popular research direction with many ICLR/ICML papers published in the past years. More importantly,  as we have argued in Related Work, leveraging ANN-to-SNN conversion can result in fast response SNN and improve the latency, both of which are required in practical applications such as edge computing.

Regarding the term "variant", we used it in a general way, to refer to the discussion that SNN was regarded as a next generation  ANN. We have now made the statement more precise in the updated version. 

**Q2: Leveraging DVS for classification itself does not make much sense. DVS is sensitive to motion, and it can provide rich temporal information but lacks texture cues. The classification does not require temporal information but requires texture cues.**

We respectfully disagree on the comment that classification task is not for DVS. First of all, this is in contrast with the current development of the field that most SNN tasks are for classifications [1-3]. We agree that DVS is sensitive to motion, but the term "motion" does not ecessarily be captured/formalised as temporal behaviour, which can only be handled well with recurrent ANN/SNN where the memory units are embedded. Instead, this paper focuses on a different way of formalising the motion in DVS, i.e., asynchronicity and sparsity, which can be dealt with non-current ANN/SNN.  

Actually, asynchronicity and sparsity lead to the lower latency and lower power in recognition system [1]. [2] has shown that the object detection with sparse events can be more computational efficiency than the traditional system --- dense and synchronous operations. These features also encourage the authors in [3] to develop an event-based dataset based on ImageNet.

In summary, while the same as other SNNs w/o memory units, our SNN is not designed for the fully temporal DVS inputs, we are exploiting the asynchronicity and sparsity of DVS inputs and achieved a performance that is superior to the state-of-the-art.  

[1] Amiret, Arnon et al. A low power, fully event-based gesture recognition system. CVPR,  2017.

[2] Messikommer, Nico  et al. Event-based asynchronous sparse convolutional networks. ECCV, 2020.

[3] Kim, Junho   et al,  N-imagenet: Towards robust, fine-grained object recognition with event cameras. CVPR, 2021.

**Q3: The author claimed that they directly process the raw events in an asynchronous manner. But, it is not clear to me how did authors achieve it.**

We do not need to take extra action/effort to obtain asynchronicity as it is a natural property of the DVS inputs. The asynchronicity can be seen by forwarding the events from DVS to SNN directly. DVS is event-driven, generating the events when the environment changes. Accordingly, the binary event with address location can be sent to its corresponding spiking neurons. The neurons only operate when they are receiving spikes. That is, the whole system is asynchronous to the environment.

**Q4: In section 4.1, the authors claimed, "When t is large enough to make $\Delta$l(t) negligible," but why?**

Equation 6 shows that $\boldsymbol{\Delta}^l(t) \triangleq  {\boldsymbol{V}^l(t)}/{(tS_r V^l_{thr})}$. According to Equation 1, we can get $\boldsymbol{V}^l(t)/V^l_{thr} \in [0,1)$. Since $S_r$ is a constant,  $\boldsymbol{\Delta}^l(t)$ tends to be zero when $t >> 1$.

**Q5: For ROE,  represents a batch of  during training. Then, it means the batch size could impact the performance of the trained model. However, the authors did not show any experimental results about it.**

The performance of ROE, like all other training schemes utilising mini-batches, is related to  the size of batches. To respond to your comment, we have now updated the Appendix to include an experiment on batch size in Figure A-6.

The result indicates that the change of $\alpha$ and batch size can influence the performance of the resulted SNN. We can see that SNN with ROE can achieve better accuracy at $0.125T_{total}$ with larger batch size. However, too small or too large batch size may significantly degrade the normal ANN training. Thus, we set the batch size wisely that can result in an optimal SNN.

content.title: Many disagreement!
content.comment:
Thanks for the feedback! But I disagree with many points of the rebuttal!

"Actually, ANN-to-SNN conversion is a popular research direction with many ICLR/ICML papers published in the past years." It does not make sense to me! ANN-to-SNN itself should not even be a topic of SNN study. SNNs leverage the bioplausible, especially for the temporal domain. ANN cannot really learn the dynamic of the temporal part. As such, ANN-to-SNN does not make sense from a bioplausible perspective. The fact that many accepted papers leverage ANN-to-SNN is true, but it does not mean ANN-to-SNN is meaningful! 

Thanks for pointing out the "N-imagenet", I think it is necessary to test the proposed approach on the N-imagenet dataset. The authors also pointed out, "A low power, fully event-based gesture recognition system." The approach requires a sequence
for capturing the temporal information, which makes sense to me! However, the other two classification tasks used in the submission do not require temporal information. BTW, the energy-efficiency is mainly introduced by TrueNorth hardware.    

Recently, many papers have leveraged SNN for robotic control tasks. I would suggest the authors check the following papers. 
1. Reinforcement co-learning of deep and spiking neural networks for energy-efficient mapless navigation with neuromorphic hardware. 
2. Deep reinforcement learning with population-coded spiking neural network for continuous control.
3. Biologically Inspired Dynamic Thresholds for Spiking Neural Networks.

Based on the feedback, I feel the authors do not deeply understand SNNs. SNNs are not a variant of ANN in general, either! SNNs themselves, without recurrent, can deal with temporal information, which can be achieved by the membrane potential accumulation and dynamic threshold.  

My question on directly processing asynchronous output from a DVS camera is about something other than where the asynchronous is from. Did the authors process each DVS pixel using a single IF neuron? In addition, "generating the events when the environment changes" is inaccurate! Camera movement can also trigger events. 

There is no experimental evidence to show the proposed approach is practical with LIF. 

Therefore, I keep my original score and do not suggest accepting submissions.

content.title: Response to Reviewer ozZz (1/2) - II
content.comment:
We appreciate you further comments and would like to address your questions as follows. 

**Q1: ANN-to-SNN itself should not even be a topic of SNN study. SNNs leverage the bioplausible, especially for the temporal domain. ANN cannot really learn the dynamic of the temporal part. As such, ANN-to-SNN does not make sense from a bioplausible perspective. The fact that many accepted papers leverage ANN-to-SNN is true, but it does not mean ANN-to-SNN is meaningful!**

We agree with you that the plausibility is an important feature in SNN, which makes SNN different from ANN. For example, the adaptive threshold benefits SNN in processing temporal information. However, in our work, we are focusing on another significant feature of SNN --- asynchronicity. This feature also differentiates SNN from ANN, and together with our cutoff, it makes SNNs adaptive in inference time and reduces the average latency. 

We respectfully disagree with you that ANN-to-SNN is not meaningful. ANN-to-SNN technique manifest the mature training regime of SNN and bridges the gap between ANN and SNN. To optimise event-driven or asynchronous SNN, as the first attempt, we choose IF neuron as our objective, due to its simplicity, while leveraging the techniques from ANN to improve the theoretical lower bound of SNN toward processing event-based input. The theoretical analysis proposed a new metric - the ratio of threshold to accumulated current - to estimate the performance of SNN. This is not in conflict with extension to other SNN neurons in the future when considering biological plausibility. 

Furthermore, although direct training of SNN considers the biological plausibility during training, it suffers from large memory consuming to train a fast response SNN, which has been argued in our related work. As an evidence, we also have shown that our SNN outperform those LIF-based SNNs using direct training in Table 2, including the results on DVS Gesture. It should be noted that we applied temporal training to ANN-to-SNN to minimise the limitation of ANN-to-SNN in processing temporal input. Figure A-2 in appendix represents the impact of temporal training. 

**Q2: N-imagenet**

We have updated our manuscript to include the reference and will consider it in our future work.

**Q3: The authors also pointed out, "A low power, fully event-based gesture recognition system." The approach requires a sequence for capturing the temporal information, which makes sense to me! However, the other two classification tasks used in the submission do not require temporal information.**

Even for Cifar10-DVS and N-Caltech101 where non-temporal information dominates, they are still characterized by asynchronicity and sparsity. In our work, we are focusing on optimising SNN for event-based input with optimal adaptive inference time.

**Q4: BTW, the energy-efficiency is mainly introduced by TrueNorth hardware.**

We believe that the energy-efficiency in TrueNorth is due to the event-driven manner of SNN. The statement below can found in supplementary of [1].

'The TrueNorth architecture aims to minimize active power using an event-driven design.

Despite using a synchronous flow, the neuron circuit operates in an event-driven manner. That is, the neuron’s clock is generated by the asynchronous Controller block, which issues on-the-fly clock pulses only when necessary for the neuron to execute synaptic integration, leak subtraction, and threshold checking.' 

[1] A million spiking-neuron integrated circuit with a scalable communication network and interface, Science, 2014

content.title: Response to Reviewer ozZz (2/2) - II
content.comment:
**Q5: SNN for robotic control tasks.**

Thanks for the suggested reference. In addition to studying plausibility of SNNs in robotic control, it will be interesting in the future to validate our cutoff in robot control tasks and see if robot control can benefit from adaptive inference time.

**Q6: SNNs themselves, without recurrent, can deal with temporal information, which can be achieved by the membrane potential accumulation and dynamic threshold.**

We do agree with you that the accumulation of membrane potential does affect the temporal prediction. However, we guess (please let us know if we didn't get your point correctly) that "temporal information" you mentioned is about the input dominated by temporal information, such as audio. At this point, we believe that deploying recurrent connection is essential for SNN to achieve high accuracy for such input, which has been introduced in [2]. Note that, the dataset in [2] has small spatial dimension but rich sequential information. In contrast, DVS has much larger spatial resolution, e.g., $128\times128\times2$ for the benchmark in our work. This physical feature in DVS allows us to consider more spatial information during processing.  

[2] Accurate and efficient time-domain classification with adaptive spiking recurrent neural networks, Nature Machine Intelligence, 2021

**Q7: Did the authors process each DVS pixel using a single IF neuron?**

In our work, the input events in one pixel can be regarded as the spikes generated in one neuron and sent to post IF neurons. 

**Q8: In addition, "generating the events when the environment changes" is inaccurate! Camera movement can also trigger events.**

The change of environment is relative to camera. 

We hope our new answers have addressed you concerns. Please let us know if you have further questions, the discussion is warmly welcomed that helps improve our work.
